title: The Glasshouse of Anderlecht
premise: Jonah Eastwick, once the conservatory's most celebrated young composer, returns to the Glasshouse of Anderlecht not as a musician but as its night janitor, hiding behind a mop and a meticulous mental inventory of everything left unsaid between them and their estranged mentor, Marta Voss. When a late-night radio broadcast airs a song Jonah wrote at seventeen—a song never recorded, never performed, kept only in a notebook Marta was supposed to have burned—Jonah realizes Marta has been quietly preserving their work all along, even as she lies dying in the building's upper flat. As Jonah cleans the rooms where their old life happened, they uncover letters, photographs, and a final unfinished score that reveals how Marta's ambition once consumed both of them. In the end, Jonah must choose whether to finish Marta's last piece under their own name or let it die with her, and by performing it in the Glasshouse with Marta listening from her deathbed, they forgive the stranger in the photographs—both of them—and finally claim the inheritance she was too proud to hand over directly.
about_author: Juniper Lockridge is the pen name of a former conservatory caretaker who spent a decade sweeping concert halls before turning to fiction. Their stories examine the quiet violence of institutions and the people who keep them running after the famous have gone home.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. On their first night shift, Jonah catalogs the Glasshouse room by room—the rehearsal halls, the locked archive, the stairwell to Marta's flat—while avoiding every place their old life might surface. The emotional beat is guarded numbness: Jonah has returned to disappear, and the chapter establishes the careful rituals that make invisibility feel like safety.

chapters.title: Static on the Third Frequency
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. Mopping the lobby past midnight, Jonah hears a radio segment featuring an 'unattributed manuscript' from the conservatory's archive—their own unpublished song, note for note. The beat is vertigo: the past has found a voice without permission, and Jonah's first instinct is to find who leaked it and destroy the trail.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Kept Everything
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. Jonah confronts the archivist, Lena, and learns the recording came from Marta's private collection, donated years ago with strict instructions. Climbing toward Marta's flat, Jonah loses their nerve at the door. The beat is dread mixed with longing—the first crack in the wall Jonah built.

chapters.title: Photographs of a Stranger
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. Cleaning Marta's office while she sleeps upstairs, Jonah finds a photograph of themselves at sixteen beside Marta, both radiant, and beneath it a letter begun and abandoned a dozen times. The beat is grief surfacing through anger as Jonah begins to see Marta as a person rather than a wound.

chapters.title: What the Board Wants
chapters.summary: POV: alternating Jonah and brief interludes from board chair Hendrik Delacroix. The conservatory's trustees plan to sell the aging Glasshouse to developers, and Delacroix discovers Marta's archive could raise its cultural value—or bury it. The beat is institutional menace: power moves quietly, and Jonah realizes the building's fate is entangled with their own buried name.

chapters.title: The Unfinished Score
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. Marta, lucid for one afternoon, summons Jonah and shows them her final composition—incomplete, built around the melody of Jonah's stolen song, meant as a duet across decades. She asks nothing; she simply leaves the pages open. The beat is trembling possibility, undercut by Marta's pride and Jonah's fear of being seen again.

chapters.title: Burning Season
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. Delacroix pressures the dying Marta to sign away rights to the archive, and Jonah intercepts the papers, discovering decades of letters in which Marta fought to protect Jonah's work from exploitation—including Delacroix's own earlier schemes. The beat is rising fury and clarity: the corruption was never just Marta's; it was the institution's.

chapters.title: Everything Unsaid
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. A midnight confrontation in Marta's sickroom: accusations, confessions, the truth about why Marta never published the song and why Jonah truly fled. Both say the unforgivable and the long-overdue. The beat is catharsis without resolution—they part still wounded, but no longer strangers.

chapters.title: The Glasshouse, Full
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. With the sale vote looming, Jonah finishes Marta's score and, defying anonymity, performs it publicly in the Glasshouse's main hall—staff, students, and Delacroix among the audience—with Marta carried down to listen. The beat is the climax: exposure as liberation, the music reclaiming both their names at once.

chapters.title: Inheritance
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. After Marta's death, the archive passes to Jonah, who chooses to endow it openly under both their names, keeping the Glasshouse alive as a public conservatory. Jonah signs the inventory ledger with their full name for the first time. The beat is quiet restoration: belonging claimed, not granted; forgiveness completed, not forgotten.
